g.text: Fixes: compression, store only frequently used data in RAM, rest on disk
"single server isn't enough" → leads into distributed store
CA: not realistic in distributed systems (network partitions always possible)
clockwise on ring, here is n is
W + R > N → strong consistency tradeoff
Temporary failures: sloppy quorum + hinted handoff
Every node keeps a membership list with a heartbeat counter for each peer.
Once every second or so, a node picks 1-3 random peers and exchanges its membership list with them,
merging in whichever heartbeat counts are newer. Because each round spreads info to new random peers,
knowledge of "who's alive" propagates exponentially — like a rumor — until the whole cluster converges
without any central coordinator. If a node's heartbeat hasn't increased for a threshold time, it's marked down.
Normal quorum reads/writes require exactly the N nodes that "own" a key on the hash ring.
Sloppy quorum relaxes this: if one of those N nodes is down, the request just uses the next healthy node on
the ring instead — so you always get W or R responses to satisfy the quorum, even during a partition.
This trades strict correctness for availability: you might read slightly stale data, but writes never block
just because one designated node is unreachable.
This is the mechanism that makes sloppy quorum work correctly. When a write lands on a
substitute node (because the real owner is down), that substitute stores the data along with a
"hint" metadata tag saying which node it actually belongs to. It's a temporary parking spot, not a
permanent replica. Once the original node recovers, the substitute node detects this (via gossip) and
forwards the hinted data back, then deletes its own copy. Net effect: no write is lost, and data
eventually lands back where it belongs.
When a node is down long enough that hinted handoff isn't enough (or data has diverged in general),
replicas run anti-entropy — a background sync process that compares two replicas' data and reconciles
differences. Comparing every key directly is too slow, so each replica builds a Merkle tree: leaves are
hashes of small key ranges, and each parent is a hash of its children, all the way up to one root hash.
Two replicas start by comparing root hashes — if equal, they're identical, done. If not, they recurse
down only the branches whose hashes differ, quickly isolating just the handful of keys that actually
changed instead of scanning the whole dataset.
